Show both paths . Step 1 — Download the data Download the files of the dataset you want to use and place them in a folder named after the dataset ( clisson/ or montagne/ ). These files are stored with Git LFS; the links below download the real content directly. Dataset Scene Typical run time (NoiseModelling) Folder Clisson Road-traffic noise map (line sources) ~15 min clisson/ La Montagne Single point source (a siren on a roof) < 1 min montagne/ Clisson — put these files in a folder named clisson/ File Size Link BUILDINGS.geojson 10.9 MB — DEM.geojson 652 MB large file — GROUNDS.geojson 9.7 MB — LW_ROADS.geojson 3.1 MB — RECEIVERS.geojson 4.6 MB — La Montagne — put these files in a folder named montagne/ File Size Link BUILDINGS.geojson 6.4 MB — DEM.geojson 219 MB large file — GROUNDS.geojson 1.4 MB — LW_ROADS.geojson 359 B — RECEIVERS.geojson 3.0 KB — Large files: the DEM files are big (652 MB for Clisson, 219 MB for La Montagne) and can take a while to download — the other files are small. Clisson is a realistic road-traffic scene (many line sources): a full NoiseModelling run takes several minutes. La Montagne is a single point source (a siren on a roof) with only 10 receivers: it runs in under a minute, which makes it ideal for a first comparison. Step 2 — Run your own software Run your model on the dataset. The comparison works at the receiver level, so your software must produce one sound level per receiver . Export a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with one point per receiver, using exactly these two properties: IDRECEIVER — the receiver identifier. It is the PK value already present in the dataset's RECEIVERS.geojson (Clisson: 0…29410, La Montagne: 1…10). LAEQ — the computed A-weighted sound level in dB at that receiver. Expected output format (one feature per receiver) copy { "type": "Feature", "properties": { "IDRECEIVER": 10, "LAEQ": 84.2 }, "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [345560.7, <sha>.6] } } For Clisson you can optionally add "PERIOD": "D" and the octave-band levels ( HZ63 … HZ8000 ) like the reference output; only IDRECEIVER and LAEQ are required for the comparison. Path A — Download the NoiseModelling reference Following Path A . Show Path B instead · Show both The benchmark already publishes the NoiseModelling output for each dataset. Download the RECEIVERS_LEVEL.geojson of the latest release (v6.0.1) — no installation, no computation needed: Dataset Reference output Clisson RECEIVERS_LEVEL.geojson La Montagne RECEIVERS_LEVEL.geojson You can also share your results with the community, or download the reference above to compare it yourself with your own software. Then go to Step 4 — Compare the two files . Path B — Run NoiseModelling yourself Following Path B . Show Path A instead · Show both B.1 — Install Java. The portable NoiseModelling_*.zip does not include Java. Install Java 25 or later (the version required by v6.0.1) from Eclipse Temurin , then check the installation: Check Java copy java -version On Windows and macOS, NoiseModelling also provides installers ( NoiseModelling-*.exe / NoiseModelling-*.dmg ) that include Java, but they install the graphical application. This path uses the command line, delivered as the portable zip. B.2 — Download NoiseModelling v6.0.1 and unzip it next to your dataset folder: Linux / macOS copy # Linux / macOS curl -L -o noisemodelling-scripts-6.0.1.zip "https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/noise-planet/noisemodelling-scripts/6.0.1/noisemodelling-scripts-6.0.1.zip" unzip noisemodelling-scripts-6.0.1.zip -d NoiseModelling Windows PowerShell copy # Windows PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/noise-planet/noisemodelling-scripts/6.0.1/noisemodelling-scripts-6.0.1.zip" -OutFile "noisemodelling-scripts-6.0.1.zip" Expand-Archive "noisemodelling-scripts-6.0.1.zip" -DestinationPath "NoiseModelling" B.3 — Download the script, put it next to the dataset folder, then run it: Clisson: compare_clisson.groovy La Montagne: compare_montagne.groovy Linux / macOS copy # Linux / macOS — run from the folder that contains clisson/ and compare_clisson.groovy NoiseModelling/bin/ScriptRunner -w workspace -s compare_clisson.groovy Windows (cmd) copy REM Windows (cmd) — run from the folder that contains clisson\ and compare_clisson.groovy NoiseModelling\bin\ScriptRunner.bat -w workspace -s compare_clisson.groovy Windows (PowerShell) copy # Windows (PowerShell) — run from the folder that contains clisson\ and compare_clisson.groovy .\NoiseModelling\bin\ScriptRunner.bat -w workspace -s compare_clisson.groovy For La Montagne, use compare_montagne.groovy instead of compare_clisson.groovy (and the montagne/ folder). The script writes output/RECEIVERS_LEVEL.geojson . Step 4 — Compare the two files Join your output with the NoiseModelling reference on IDRECEIVER and compare the LAEQ values. Two rules matter for a fair comparison: Silence threshold. In the benchmark, levels at or below −89 dB are treated as silence and excluded from the statistics. Apply the same rule. La Montagne calibration. The published La Montagne comparison is calibrated per version: an offset is applied so that the computed level equals the measured level at the receiver closest to the source. The raw output is not calibrated — calibration is only used on the results page. Share your results with the community Comparing independent implementations is how the community finds bugs and improves the models. If you would like to share your run, copy the template below into an issue on this repository (or a pull request). We would be delighted! Troubleshooting “java: command not found” — Java is not installed or not on your PATH (Path B only). Reopen your terminal after installing it. “Unsupported class file major version” — you are using an older Java. Install Java 25 or later. Step 2 — Run your own software Run your model on the dataset. The comparison works at the receiver level, so your software must produce one sound level per receiver . Export a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with one point per receiver, using exactly these two properties: IDRECEIVER — the receiver identifier. It is the PK value already present in the dataset's RECEIVERS.geojson (Clisson: 0…29410, La Montagne: 1…10). LAEQ — the computed A-weighted sound level in dB at that receiver. Expected output format (one feature per receiver) copy { "type": "Feature", "properties": { "IDRECEIVER": 10, "LAEQ": 84.2 }, "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [345560.7, <sha>.6] } } For Clisson you can optionally add "PERIOD": "D" and the octave-band levels ( HZ63 … HZ8000 ) like the reference output; only IDRECEIVER and LAEQ are required for the comparison. The script writes output/RECEIVERS_LEVEL.geojson . Step 4 — Compare the two files Join your output with the NoiseModelling reference on IDRECEIVER and compare the LAEQ values. Two rules matter for a fair comparison: Silence threshold. In the benchmark, levels at or below −89 dB are treated as silence and excluded from the statistics. Apply the same rule. La Montagne calibration. The published La Montagne comparison is calibrated per version: an offset is applied so that the computed level equals the measured level at the receiver closest to the source. The raw output is not calibrated — calibration is only used on the results page.
